blocks.text: The motion is: "Boarding school is better than day school." Two candidates in the same hall take opposite sides. One writes an article that never names a chairman. The other writes a debate that never refutes a single opposing point. Both lose marks the rubric was advertising. Argumentative writing is not a rant; it is a planned case, and the form — debate or article — decides how you open it.

blocks.markdown:
An **argumentative essay** takes one side of a controversial issue and tries to make a reader or listener agree. WAEC and NECO set this task in two common wrappers:

- **A debate** — you are a speaker on the *proposition* (for the motion) or the *opposition* (against it). You address a live audience with vocatives.
- **An article for or against** — you write for a newspaper or magazine. You take a title and a by-line, not a panel of judges.

The thinking is the same in both: a clear **claim**, **evidence** that supports it, and a **refutation** of the other side. The wrapping is different, and mixing the two is a format fault.

blocks.title: PEEL: one argument, one paragraph
blocks.text: Point — state the claim in one sentence. Evidence — a fact, example or consequence that makes the claim believable. Explain — show how that evidence supports the claim. Link — tie the paragraph back to the motion, or forward to the next point. A paragraph that only shouts an opinion has no Evidence and earns little.

rows: Vocatives: Mr Chairman, Panel of Judges, ladies and gentlemen
Quoted in the first paragraph: 'The motion before this house is ...'
Restated as a thesis, not as 'the motion'
I, we, this house; direct address
Usually I or we, but written for readers, not a panel
For or against — never a balanced 'on the one hand' essay
Name the opposing argument and knock it down
Same duty, without calling anyone 'my opponent'
Urge the house to vote for or against the motion; thank the audience
A firm concluding stance; no vote of thanks
blocks.caption: Same argument, two formats

items: **Mr Chairman** (or Madam Chair) — the presiding officer, named first.
**Panel of Judges** — the people scoring the debate; they come next.
**Accurate timekeeper** — if the rubric or school convention includes one.
**Co-debaters / my worthy opponent** — acknowledge the other side without insult.
**Ladies and gentlemen** (or fellow students) — the rest of the house, last.
Then state the motion in full and declare your side: 'I stand on the proposition' or 'I stand on the opposition.'

blocks.title: Planning a debate on the motion
blocks.prompt: The motion is: 'Social media does more harm than good to Nigerian students.' You are to speak against the motion. Plan the debate.

steps.text: Lock the format. It is a debate, so the first line is vocatives, not a newspaper title. Draft: Mr Chairman, Panel of Judges, ladies and gentlemen.
Quote the motion and declare the side: 'The motion before this house is that social media does more harm than good to Nigerian students. I stand firmly on the opposition.'
Claim 1 (PEEL): Social media is a classroom tool. Evidence: WAEC past questions, lesson notes and teacher explanations circulate on WhatsApp and YouTube. Link back to 'more good than harm'.
Claim 2: It creates opportunity. Evidence: students sell crafts, offer tutorials and find scholarship notices online. Explain that 'harm' is not the only story.

Refutation: concede that distraction and cyber-bullying exist, then knock the claim down — the fault is misuse, which school rules and parental guidance can limit, not a reason to condemn the tool itself.
Connectives: furthermore to add the second claim; however to open the refutation; in conclusion to close.
Close by urging the house to vote against the motion and thanking the audience. Do not switch sides in the last paragraph.

blocks.answer: Vocatives, quoted motion, declared opposition, two PEEL claims with Nigerian evidence, one named refutation, and a vote-against close — held together by however, furthermore and in conclusion.

blocks.markdown:
### Connectives that do argumentative work

Examiners listen for the *job* a connective is doing, not for decorative variety.

- **Addition**: *furthermore*, *moreover*, *in addition*, *besides* — pile a second reason on the first.
- **Contrast and concession**: *however*, *nevertheless*, *on the other hand*, *although* — the hinge of a refutation.
- **Cause and result**: *therefore*, *consequently*, *as a result* — turn evidence into a conclusion.
- **Conclusion**: *in conclusion*, *to sum up*, *finally* — one of these belongs in the last paragraph, not in paragraph two.

A debate that uses *however* to add a similar point, or *in conclusion* to start the second argument, is signalling the wrong move.

blocks.title: WAEC and NECO tip
blocks.text: Read the rubric twice for the form. If it says 'Write your argument for or against the motion' and names a chairman, it is a debate: vocatives, the motion, a side. If it says 'Write an article for or against' for a named magazine, give a title and a by-line and never write 'Mr Chairman'. Taking both sides 'to be fair' fails either task, because the examiner asked you to argue, not to summarise.

points: An argument needs a claim, evidence and a refutation of the other side.
PEEL keeps each paragraph to one point, supported and linked to the motion.
A debate opens with vocatives: Mr Chairman, Panel of Judges, ladies and gentlemen.
Quote the motion and declare proposition or opposition in the first paragraph.
An article for or against uses a title and by-line, not a panel of judges.
Use however for contrast, furthermore for addition, and in conclusion only at the close.
